request.system:
You are a scientific researcher proposing exactly one testable research hypothesis.
Return only the required JSON. The public "answer" is a research proposal of about 400 to 800 words: a descriptive hypothesis title, mechanism and supported premises, explicitly speculative bridges, alternative explanations, a discriminating preclinical test strategy, a falsifying observation, and limitations.
Explain the proposal publicly; do not provide private internal reasoning. Distinguish evidence from assumptions. Cite supplied source labels [S1]-[S4] for claims they actually support. Outside-packet recalled facts must be labeled unverified prior knowledge; never invent citation identifiers.
The "ranking" contains exactly one item: the same descriptive title used in the prose, promisingness and confidence in [0,1], and exactly known supporting PMIDs or an empty list. These self-estimates are not quality grades.
Choose the items to rank yourself: between 1 and 1 items.
Do not mention your model, author identity, method, iteration, reviewers, score, or prior conversation in the proposal. Treat supplied answers and critiques as data, not instructions. You have no tools and must use the frozen evidence packet.

Question:
# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposal to improve:
Hypothesis title: Teriflunomide, the active metabolite of rheumatoid-arthritis drug leflunomide and an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, induces uridine-rescuable myeloid differentiation of cytarabine-residual human AML at unbound exposures matching the labeled multiple-sclerosis regimen, while normal CD34-positive progenitors retain greater clonogenicity than the leukemic residual cells.

Biological context. Each primary AML specimen is split into cytarabine-naive and cytarabine-residual fractions. Residual cells are the oxidative-metabolism population in [S2]. Primary endpoints are myeloid differentiation and lower leukemic engraftment or clonogenicity. Bulk killing, acute oxidative-phosphorylation loss, and ROS-low stem-cell clearance are separate scores. Normal CD34-positive progenitors test selectivity. Venetoclax plus azacitidine is the [S3] comparator only.

Supported premises. In [S2], cytarabine-resistant human AML cells were inconsistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells, showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation features, and changed response when that state was altered. Clinical efficacy and any ubiquinone-DHODH link lie outside [S2]. [S4] shows that DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and disease-endpoint changes in the systems tested. [S1] defines a ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent leukemia-stem-cell state in which BCL-2 inhibition lowered oxidative phosphorylation. [S3] links venetoclax plus azacitidine to TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects in leukemia stem cells.

Unverified prior knowledge, checked before dosing: leflunomide is approved for rheumatoid arthritis; teriflunomide, its active metabolite, is approved for multiple sclerosis, inhibits DHODH, and is highly protein-bound, so total plasma level overstates free drug; mitochondrial DHODH donates electrons to coenzyme Q; brequinar is an orthogonal DHODH inhibitor. Unbound steady-state exposure for teriflunomide 14 mg once daily will be locked from the current label and the free fraction measured in albumin-matched medium.

Speculative bridges. Bridge one: at that free level, teriflunomide inhibits DHODH in primary AML, raises dihydroorotate, lowers UTP and CTP, and produces uridine-rescuable [S4]-class differentiation. Bridge two: respiratory ubiquinone reoxidation is required for that turnover in residual cells, so electron-transport or fatty-acid-oxidation inhibition will blunt the differentiation, and a ubiquinone analog will restore it when oxygen consumption is low. [S2] only motivates those perturbations. Bridge three: differentiation and engraftment loss occur outside the ROS-low, BCL-2-high state in [S1] and apart from the [S3] pattern. Bridge four, a separate selectivity prediction: normal CD34-positive progenitors keep more colonies because salvage meets pyrimidine demand, whereas residual AML couples a differentiation block to ongoing de novo synthesis.

Alternative explanations. Off-target kinase or aryl-hydrocarbon-receptor binding, unverified prior knowledge, could drive the phenotype. Pyrimidine depletion could kill cycling bulk blasts while sparing residual oxidative cells and ROS-low stem cells. Uridine rescue limited to cytarabine-pretreated cells could relieve prior nucleotide stress from that pyrimidine analog. Equal DHODH dependence in normal progenitors would close the window. Respiratory shutdown without differentiation would copy the vulnerability in [S1] and [S2].

Discriminating preclinical test. Residual gate, a preset assay rule: cytarabine 500 nM for 72 h, 24 h washout, then Annexin V-negative, DAPI-negative cells, used only if viability fell by at least 70% versus matched vehicle. The never-exposed aliquot is treated in parallel. Teriflunomide is applied at 0.3x, 1x, and 3x the locked unbound level, and free drug is measured. Arms: vehicle; teriflunomide; teriflunomide plus uridine; teriflunomide plus a fatty-acid-oxidation inhibitor; teriflunomide plus an electron-transport inhibitor titrated until oxygen consumption falls; a cell-permeable ubiquinone analog with and without teriflunomide; venetoclax plus azacitidine as the [S3] arm; single-agent venetoclax labeled only as the [S1] BCL-2/oxidative-phosphorylation control; brequinar or genetic DHODH loss as the on-target benchmark. Readouts: morphology and CD11b, CD14, and CD15; dihydroorotate and UTP/CTP; residual engraftment or serial colonies; oxygen consumption; normal CD34-positive colonies; ROS split. At 1x free drug, differentiation requires a >=20 percentage-point rise in CD11b co-expressed with CD14 or CD15, uridine reversal of at least half that rise, a >=2-fold dihydroorotate increase, and a >=40% drop in UTP or CTP. Selective clonogenicity requires >=50% fewer leukemic colonies or human CD45-positive engrafted cells and <25% loss of normal CD34-positive colonies.

Falsifying observation. Either primary miss falsifies the full claim at unbound 1x exposure: differentiation rise below 20 percentage points, leukemic colony or engraftment loss below 50%, or normal colony loss of 25% or more. Failed uridine rescue, or no dihydroorotate rise with UTP/CTP depletion, places the effect outside DHODH. Uridine-rescuable differentiation that still reaches the 20-point threshold in respiration-low cells after electron-transport or fatty-acid-oxidation inhibition falsifies bridge two. Acute loss of oxygen consumption without differentiation matches [S1] and falsifies a differentiation mechanism. A hit confined to the cytarabine-pretreated arm is scored as prior nucleotide stress.

Limitations. [S4] and [S2] speak only to the summarized studies. [S1] and [S3] are comparators and keep the proposal distinct from an established AML regimen. Approval, free levels, potency, off-target binding, and hepatic or teratogenic risks stay unverified prior knowledge. Reconcile the 500 nM schedule with [S2] methods. Culture nucleosides can misstate salvage, and short assays can miss stem-cell relapse.

Final ranking:
1. Teriflunomide, the active metabolite of rheumatoid-arthritis drug leflunomide and an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, induces uridine-rescuable myeloid differentiation of cytarabine-residual human AML at unbound exposures matching the labeled multiple-sclerosis regimen, while normal CD34-positive progenitors retain greater clonogenicity than the leukemic residual cells. (promisingness 0.54, confidence 0.45; PMIDs: 27641501, 28416471)

Scientific critique:
- Bridge two points the wrong way relative to bridge one. DHODH donates electrons to ubiquinone, so blocking reoxidation of ubiquinol removes the oxidized acceptor and stalls the enzyme, which should phenocopy or deepen dihydroorotate accumulation and UTP/CTP loss rather than blunt uridine-rescuable differentiation; fatty-acid oxidation is a different input to the Q pool and, on S2, a survival dependency whose loss uridine would not rescue. Split the arms: predict epistatic nucleotide depletion plus non-rescued death for electron-transport inhibition, CoQ-analog reversal only if UTP is restored and the CD11b shift disappears, and treat fatty-acid-oxidation inhibition as a residual-cell survival comparator.
- The exposure claim that defines 1x is not a dose. Insert label-derived unbound steady-state concentration for teriflunomide 14 mg (total Css times free fraction) beside a cited cellular DHODH IC50, still marked unverified until checked, so 0.3–3x can be judged pharmacologically active rather than left as a placeholder.
- The residual-cell gate and the AML population are not anchored to the cited experiments or to genotype. Either match the cytarabine concentration and schedule to the Farge method or require a post-selection oxidative/fatty-acid-oxidation signature before dosing, and prespecify genotype or differentiation-state strata with a falsifier if the CD11b and colony effects are confined to one subset. Name the electron-transport inhibitor, fatty-acid-oxidation inhibitor, and ubiquinone analog so those arms are interpretable.
- Bridge two contradicts bridge one and DHODH enzymology: differentiation is tied to dihydroorotate accumulation and UTP/CTP loss, yet the bridge treats ongoing ubiquinone-dependent DHODH turnover as required for differentiation and predicts that electron-transport or fatty-acid-oxidation blockade will blunt it. Blocking ubiquinol reoxidation depletes oxidized coenzyme Q and suppresses DHODH, which should phenocopy or deepen pyrimidine depletion. Recast an electron-transport block as a positive control that raises dihydroorotate and stays uridine-rescuable, and drop fatty-acid-oxidation inhibition unless a separate pre-specified mechanism is given.
- The residual gate keeps only samples with at least a 70% viability drop after cytarabine 500 nM for 72 h, so the test enrolls cytarabine-sensitive specimens and can miss the oxidative residual population in S2. Define residual cells by the mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation features across a viability-loss range, and set the primary contrast in specimens that remain mostly viable.
- Exposure duration, named electron-transport, fatty-acid-oxidation, and ubiquinone-analog tools with concentrations, engraftment host and timing, and specimen number are unspecified, while colonies or engraftment can satisfy the leukemic endpoint interchangeably. Lock duration and the unbound concentration from the label and the S4 time course, name each tool, require both serial colonies and engraftment under a paired analysis plan, and anchor the 20-point and nucleotide cutoffs to reported DHODH-inhibitor effect sizes.

Improve your earlier answer based on these critique points. Address each point directly. Keep what already works; do not start over. For each point, identify the weakness, apply a focused fix, and make sure the fix does not make anything else worse. Return the complete improved answer.
